1 Vectors

1.1 Create a numeric vector called “stock_prices” with the following data points: 42.5, 43.0, 44.1, and 2.7. Next, verify the class of it.

```{r}
# Create a numeric vector of stock prices
stock_prices <- c(42.5, 43.0, 44.1, 2.7)

# Print the vector to confirm it was created correctly
stock_prices

# Verify the class of the vector
class(stock_prices)
```
[1] 42.5 43.0 44.1  2.7
[1] "numeric"

1.2 Create a character vector called “company_names” with the following data points: “Apple”, “Google”, “Microsoft”, and “Tesla”.

```{r}
# Create a character vector of company names
stock_company <- c("Microsoft", "Apple", "Facebook", "Tesla")

# Print the vector to confirm it was created correctly
stock_company
```
[1] "Microsoft" "Apple"     "Facebook"  "Tesla"

1.3 Create a character vector called “stock_ticker” consisting of stock tickers corresponding to the companies in the “stock_company” vector: MSFT, AAPL, FB, and TSLA. Then verify its data type.

```{r}
# Create a character vector of stock tickers
stock_ticker <- c("MSFT", "AAPL", "FB", "TSLA")

# Print the vector to confirm it was created correctly
stock_ticker

# Verify the data type / class
class(stock_ticker)
```
[1] "MSFT" "AAPL" "FB"   "TSLA"
[1] "character"

1.4 Create a logical vector called “make_cars” consisting of the four logical values: FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, and TRUE.

```{r}
# Create a logical vector showing whether each company makes cars
make_cars <- c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE)

# Print the vector to confirm it was created correctly
make_cars

# Verify the class
class(make_cars)
```
[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
[1] "logical"

1.5 After that, add 5 to the vector “stock_prices” and assign the result to the same “stock_prices” vector, essentially updating the existing stock prices vector.

```{r}
# Add 5 to each element in the stock_prices vector and update it
stock_prices <- stock_prices + 5
# Print the updated stock_prices vector to confirm the changes
stock_prices
```
[1] 47.5 48.0 49.1  7.7

1.6 Name each element in “stock_prices” vector, using the “stock_company” vector that you created above, and print the stock_prirces vector to confirm that each element has a company name associated with it.

```{r}
# Assign company names to the stock_prices vector
names(stock_prices) <- stock_company

# Print the named vector to confirm the names were assigned
stock_prices
```
Microsoft     Apple  Facebook     Tesla 
     47.5      48.0      49.1       7.7

2 Creating and cleaning a data frame in base R

2.1 Create a data frame called “stock_info.df” which is composed of the four vectors created in exercises #2 and #3 above. Verify the number of rows and columns, and also display the summary.

```{r}
# Create a data frame using the four vectors created earlier
stock_info.df <- data.frame(
  stock_company = stock_company,
  stock_ticker = stock_ticker,
  stock_prices = stock_prices,
  make_cars = make_cars
)

# Print the data frame to confirm it was created correctly
stock_info.df

# Verify the number of rows and columns
nrow(stock_info.df)
ncol(stock_info.df)

# Display the summary of the data frame
summary(stock_info.df)
```
[1] 4
[1] 4
 stock_company      stock_ticker        stock_prices   make_cars

 Class :character   Class :character   1st Qu.:37.55   FALSE:3        
 Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Median :47.75   TRUE :1

                                       3rd Qu.:48.27                  
                                       Max.   :49.10

2.2 (1) Let’s suppose that there was a data entry error in “stock_prices” vector such that Tesla’s original stock price was 42.7, not 2.7. Also, note that previously you updated the stock price by adding 5 to all elements in the stock_prices vector, making the updated stock price of Tesla 7.7. (2) Now that we know there was a data entry error, we need to update Tesla’s stock price correctly in the data frame created earlier. In short, we need to replace 7.7 with 47.7, which would have been the correct stock price for Tesla in the previous exercise, had there not been an error in the first place. (3) Do the necessary coding to execute the correction to the stock_info.df data frame. Confirm the operation was successful by printing the data frame.

```{r}
# Correct Tesla's stock price in the data frame
stock_info.df$stock_prices[stock_info.df$stock_company == "Tesla"] <- 47.7

# Print the updated data frame to confirm the correction worked
stock_info.df
```

3 Adding a row or column to a data frame in base R

3.1 (1) Add a new row to the bottom of the existing “stock_info.df” data frame with the following information: stock_prices = 50.4, stock_company = General Motors, stock_ticker = GM, and make_cars = TRUE. (2) Print out the updated data frame. (3) Do you see the row name of the last row is “1”? You may want to replace this with the correct name, “General Motors.” Print the data frame again to confirm you fixed the problem.

```{r}
# Create a new one-row data frame for General Motors
new_row <- data.frame(
  stock_company = "General Motors",
  stock_ticker = "GM",
  stock_prices = 50.4,
  make_cars = TRUE
)

# Append the new row to the existing data frame
stock_info.df <- rbind(stock_info.df, new_row)

# Print the updated data frame
stock_info.df

# Change the row name of the last row to "General Motors"
rownames(stock_info.df)[nrow(stock_info.df)] <- "General Motors"

# Print the data frame again to confirm the row name was fixed
stock_info.df
```

3.2 (1) Add a new column with the following column name and values: open_price = 47.3, 47.8, 49.5, 47.9 and 55.3. (2) Print out the updated data frame, “stock_info.df” to confirm your work.

```{r}
# Add a new column called open_price
stock_info.df$open_price <- c(47.3, 47.8, 49.5, 47.9, 55.3)

# Print the updated data frame to confirm the new column was added
stock_info.df
```

4 Creating a new column from existing columns and subsetting

4.1 Now, create a new vector called “change_stock_prices_percent” and add it to the existing data frame to show if the stock increased or decreased its price at the end of the day compared to the beginning of the day.

```{r}
# Calculate the percent change from open price to closing price
change_stock_prices_percent <- ((stock_info.df$stock_prices - stock_info.df$open_price) / stock_info.df$open_price) * 100

# Add the new vector as a column in the data frame
stock_info.df$change_stock_prices_percent <- change_stock_prices_percent

# Print the updated data frame to confirm the new column was added
stock_info.df
```

4.2 Which stock has increased its value and which ones have decreased? Use the function “subset” to select the two types of stocks.

```{r}
# Subset stocks that increased in value
stocks_increased <- subset(stock_info.df, change_stock_prices_percent > 0)

# Print stocks that increased
stocks_increased

# Subset stocks that decreased in value
stocks_decreased <- subset(stock_info.df, change_stock_prices_percent < 0)

# Print stocks that decreased
stocks_decreased
```

5 Matrix

Create a matrix named “odd.mat” that consists of odd numbers starting with “1” with 10 columns and 5 rows. Do the task in both Base R and Tidyverse way, respectively.

```{r}
# Tidyverse approach:
library(tidyverse)

# Create the same sequence of odd numbers with tibble/dplyr workflow
odd_numbers_tbl <- tibble(odd_numbers = seq(from = 1, by = 2, length.out = 50))

# Convert the column to a matrix with 5 rows and 10 columns
odd.mat <- matrix(odd_numbers_tbl$odd_numbers, nrow = 5, ncol = 10)

# Print the matrix to confirm it was created correctly
odd.mat
```

```{r}
data("sentences", package = "stringr")

first_words <- word(sentences, 1, 1) %>%
  str_trim()

# Print all extracted first words to confirm the operation worked
first_words
```

  1. From the package, use “gapminder” dataset. Examine the dataset to know it first.

  3. From the most recent year in the dataset, calculate the total population by the continents and print out the outcome.
  4. Print out the continent and total population again by arranging the appearance of the continent in descending order of the size of the population.
  5. Compare both tables produced in (2) and (3) and describe how the order is different. Note that you haven’t changed the factor level yet. Also, state how you could change the level of the factor by the descending order of the population size.
  6. change the order of the level of the “continent” factor by the size of the continent’s total population and save the change made to the continent by naming the data “gapminder1”. Make sure you confirm the operation was successful.
```{r}
# Install packages if needed
install.packages("gapminder")
```

```{r}
# Load packages
library(gapminder)
library(tidyverse)

# Examine the dataset
glimpse(gapminder)

# Print the factor levels of continent
levels(gapminder$continent)

# Find the most recent year in the dataset
most_recent_year <- max(gapminder$year)

# Calculate total population by continent for the most recent year
continent_pop <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == most_recent_year) %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(total_population = sum(pop))

# Print the summary table
continent_pop

# Arrange the table in descending order of total population
continent_pop_desc <- continent_pop %>%
  arrange(desc(total_population))

# Print the arranged table
continent_pop_desc
```

Rows: 1,704
Columns: 6
$ country   <fct> "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", …
$ continent <fct> Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, …
$ year      <int> 1952, 1957, 1962, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, …
$ lifeExp   <dbl> 28.801, 30.332, 31.997, 34.020, 36.088, 38.438, 39.854, 40.8…
$ pop       <int> 8425333, 9240934, 10267083, 11537966, 13079460, 14880372, 12…

[1] "Africa"   "Americas" "Asia"     "Europe"   "Oceania"

The first table keeps the original factor order of continent, while the second table sorts the rows by total population in descending order. This means the rows are displayed differently, but the factor levels themselves have not changed yet. To change the factor levels by descending population size, I can use fct_reorder() from the forcats package and reorder continent using the total population values.

```{r}
# Create a reordered factor for continent based on total population in the most recent year
continent_order <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == most_recent_year) %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(total_population = sum(pop)) %>%
  mutate(continent = fct_reorder(continent, total_population, .desc = TRUE)) %>%
  select(continent)

# Save the reordered continent factor into a new dataset called gapminder1
gapminder1 <- gapminder %>%
  mutate(continent = factor(continent,
                            levels = levels(continent_order$continent)))

# Confirm the operation was successful by printing the new factor levels
levels(gapminder1$continent)
```
[1] "Asia"     "Africa"   "Americas" "Europe"   "Oceania"

8.2

  1. Using the original gapminder data (not gapminder1), draw a chart that shows the total population by each continent in the year 2007, ordered by the size of the population in the chart. As usual, do this in one chain of codes and provide the necessary information and beautification to the chart to portray accurate communication to the viewers.

The chart below uses the original gapminder data, filters the year 2007, calculates total population by continent, reorders the continent names within the plotting code, and creates a presentable bar chart in one chain of code

```{r}
gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007) %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(total_population = sum(pop)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(continent, total_population, .desc = TRUE),
             y = total_population,
             fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(total_population)),
            vjust = -0.3,
            size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Population by Continent in 2007",
    x = "Continent",
    y = "Total Population"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

```{r}
library(gapminder)
```

9.2 How many Asian countries do you see? Given

```{r}
gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia")
```

9.3 Given the number of countries, it seems like a good idea to present the top 5 and bottom 5 countries, one at a time, and order the countries by life expectancy. Let’s first focus on the top 5 list. Do appropriate wrangling and visualization for the top 5 list.

The code below selects the top 5 Asian countries in 2007 based on life expectancy, orders the countries by life expectancy, and creates a presentable bar chart.

```{r}
# Create the top 5 chart
top_5_asia <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") %>%
  slice_max(order_by = lifeExp, n = 5) %>%
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, lifeExp))

top_5_plot <- ggplot(top_5_asia, aes(x = country, y = lifeExp, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(lifeExp, 1)), hjust = -0.1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 5 Asian Countries by Life Expectancy in 2007",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

# Print the chart
top_5_plot
```

9.4 Do similar wrangling and visualization to show the bottom 5 countries. (5) This time, let’s put the two charts together and show them in one pallet by using the patchwork package <https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/Links to an external site.>. The end result should look like this.

The code below creates a chart for the bottom 5 Asian countries by life expectancy in 2007, and then combines the top 5 and bottom 5 charts into one display using the patchwork package.

```{r}
# Create the bottom 5 chart
bottom_5_asia <- gapminder %>%
  filter(year == 2007, continent == "Asia") %>%
  slice_min(order_by = lifeExp, n = 5) %>%
  mutate(country = fct_reorder(country, lifeExp))

bottom_5_plot <- ggplot(bottom_5_asia, aes(x = country, y = lifeExp, fill = country)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(lifeExp, 1)), hjust = -0.1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Bottom 5 Asian Countries by Life Expectancy in 2007",
    x = "Country",
    y = "Life Expectancy"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

# Print the bottom 5 chart
bottom_5_plot
```
```{r}
# Combine the two charts using patchwork
top_5_plot + bottom_5_plot
```

10.2 Include only the records that do not have missing values in the following three variables: dep_time arr_time and air_time. Convert “dep_time” and “arr_time” to date-time data type, using “year”, “month”, and “day” as well as the hour and minutes information from “dep_time” and “arr_time”. Then select only some useful columns we will need to draw a chart since there are too many columns to display. Those variables are “origin”, “dest”, “air_time”, and any variables that start with ‘dep’ or ‘arr.’ Let’s save this subset of the data as “flights_lub.”

The code below removes rows with missing values in dep_time, arr_time, and air_time. Then it converts dep_time and arr_time into proper date-time variables by combining the date columns with the hour and minute values. After that, I keep only the requested columns and save the result as flights_lub.

```{r}
# Create a cleaned subset called flights_lub
flights_lub <- flights %>%
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time), !is.na(air_time)) %>%
  mutate(
    dep_time = sprintf("%04d", dep_time),
    arr_time = sprintf("%04d", arr_time),
    dep_time = make_datetime(
      year = year,
      month = month,
      day = day,
      hour = as.numeric(substr(dep_time, 1, 2)),
      min = as.numeric(substr(dep_time, 3, 4))
    ),
    arr_time = make_datetime(
      year = year,
      month = month,
      day = day,
      hour = as.numeric(substr(arr_time, 1, 2)),
      min = as.numeric(substr(arr_time, 3, 4))
    )
  ) %>%
  select(origin, dest, air_time, starts_with("dep"), starts_with("arr"))

# Print the data to confirm the wrangling worked
flights_lub
```

10.3 Using the “dep_time” variable, display the frequency distribution of the count of flights departing from New York City over the entire year in 2013, from Jan. 1 to Dec. 31.

The chart below displays the frequency distribution of flight departures across the full year of 2013 using the dep_time variable.

```{r}
# Plot the frequency distribution of departures over the full year
ggplot(flights_lub, aes(x = dep_time)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Frequency Distribution of NYC Flight Departures in 2013",
    x = "Departure Date-Time",
    y = "Count of Flights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

10.4 This time, let’s zoom in on just one day, the Fourth of July holiday. Display the frequency distribution of the flights departing from New York City during the entire day.

The chart below focuses only on flights departing on July 4, 2013, and shows the frequency distribution during that day.

```{r}
# Plot the frequency distribution of departures on July 4, 2013
flights_lub %>%
  filter(date(dep_time) == ymd("2013-07-04")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dep_time)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24) +
  labs(
    title = "Frequency Distribution of NYC Flight Departures on July 4, 2013",
    x = "Departure Date-Time",
    y = "Count of Flights"
  ) +

```

10.5 Using the “flights_lub” dataset, create the “travel_time” variable by subtracting “dep_time” from “arr_time”. Since arrival occurs later than departure, arr_time minus dep_time should be positive. Check this logic by sorting the data by the ascending order of “travel_time” Was the expectation met? No, because you will see negative minutes of travel_time. Pay attention to the type of data for travel_time. Why were there negative minutes?

The code below creates ‘travel_time’ by subtracting ‘dep_time’ from ‘arr_time’, then sorts the data from the smallest value to the largest value. This shows that some values are negative.

```{r}
# Create travel_time and sort by ascending order
flights_lub <- flights_lub %>%
  mutate(travel_time = arr_time - dep_time)

# Print the smallest travel_time values
flights_lub %>%
  arrange(travel_time) %>%
  select(origin, dest, dep_time, arr_time, air_time, travel_time) %>%
  head(10)
```

The expectation was not met because some travel_time values are negative. The travel_time variable is a time difference object. The negative values happen because some flights are overnight flights. In those cases, the arrival time is on the next day, but the initial arr_time date was still assigned to the same day as departure.

10.6 That was because those flights were overnight flights. The original dep_time had only hour and minutes information before day information was added and the time of arrival is smaller than the time of departure for the overnight flights. Thus, we need to fix “arr_time” by adding one more day when there was such an overnight flight. Do the appropriate adjustment prior to the travel_time variable creation in the chain of codes connected through a series of pipe operators. Also, convert the travel_time to a numeric data type. Show that there are no negative minutes anymore.

```{r}
# Fix overnight flights and recalculate travel_time in minutes
flights_lub <- flights %>%
  filter(!is.na(dep_time), !is.na(arr_time), !is.na(air_time)) %>%
  mutate(
    dep_time = sprintf("%04d", dep_time),
    arr_time = sprintf("%04d", arr_time),
    dep_time = make_datetime(
      year = year,
      month = month,
      day = day,
      hour = as.numeric(substr(dep_time, 1, 2)),
      min = as.numeric(substr(dep_time, 3, 4))
    ),
    arr_time = make_datetime(
      year = year,
      month = month,
      day = day,
      hour = as.numeric(substr(arr_time, 1, 2)),
      min = as.numeric(substr(arr_time, 3, 4))
    ),
    arr_time = if_else(arr_time < dep_time, arr_time + days(1), arr_time),
    travel_time = as.numeric(difftime(arr_time, dep_time, units = "mins"))
  ) %>%
  select(origin, dest, air_time, starts_with("dep"), starts_with("arr"), travel_time)

# Print the smallest travel_time values to confirm there are no negatives
flights_lub %>%
  arrange(travel_time) %>%
  select(origin, dest, dep_time, arr_time, air_time, travel_time) %>%
  head(10)
```

10.7 Once again, zoom in on the Forth of July. How many flights departed from New York City on that day? Create a plot that shows the relationship between the “travel_time” and “air_time” What do you infer from it? Why is there not a perfect association?

The code below counts the flights on July 4, 2013, and then creates a scatterplot showing the relationship between ‘travel_time’ and ‘air_time’.

```{r}
# Count flights on July 4, 2013
flights_lub %>%
  filter(date(dep_time) == ymd("2013-07-04")) %>%
  summarise(number_of_flights = n())
# Plot the relationship between travel_time and air_time for July 4, 2013
flights_lub %>%
  filter(date(dep_time) == ymd("2013-07-04")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = air_time, y = travel_time)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Air Time and Travel Time on July 4, 2013",
    x = "Air Time (minutes)",
    y = "Travel Time (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The scatterplot should show a strong positive relationship between air_time and travel_time. This makes sense because flights that spend more time in the air usually also have longer total travel time. However, the relationship is not perfect because travel_time includes more than just time in the air. It can also reflect taxi-out time, taxi-in time, and other delays before takeoff or after landing.
